NEWS 2026-11-18 PlayFront (GTA 6 performance test: Why even the PS5 Pro is running at its limit at 30 FPS):
Digital Foundry has extensively tested the technology behind GTA 6 and finally provides a clear answer to the frame rate question. Even the PS5 Pro can't manage 60 FPS because Rockstar Games uncompromisingly invests all of its processing power in world simulation, ray tracing, and absurd details like hair physics for every single pedestrian.
Rockstar Games completely sacrifices a smooth 60 frames per second for maximum simulation of the game world. approved John Linneman of Digital Foundry after over 50 hours of gameplay on the PS5 Pro.
On the one hand, I'm deeply impressed by how uncompromisingly the atmosphere of Vice City has been crafted. On the other hand, it's painful to see even an expensive Pro console capped at 30 FPS.
Hair strands and world simulation consume frames per second.
According to the technical analysis, the reason for this slowdown lies far beneath the surface. Rockstar calculates physics-based hair strands not only for the two main characters, Jason and Lucia, but for virtually all NPCs on the streets. Each individual strand reacts separately to wind, water, and movement. This sounds like a completely crazy detail for everyday life, but it consumes a massive amount of processing power.
Furthermore, the game world doesn't simply shut down, even over great distances. This is also supported by the... international reviews of the gameTraffic and pedestrians remain constantly active, while the police plan their operations with real visual contact, fixed deployment locations and coordinated pursuits.
When you add interactive objects, dynamic destruction, detailed damage models for vehicles, and ray tracing for global illumination and reflections, the hardware is pushed to its absolute limit. The latest screenshots even showed burst blood vessels in the eyes.
Stable 30 FPS on the Pro, shaky on the base PS5
For the actual gaming experience on the couch, there is at least some good news. In over 50 hours on the PS5 Pro, GTA 6 ran almost continuously at a rock-solid 30 FPS with clean frame pacing. Only when Linneman triggered countless explosions simultaneously in a targeted extreme test did the frame rate briefly drop to 24 FPS.
On the standard PS5, the situation is considerably less smooth. According to measurements, even in ordinary gameplay situations, there are occasional slight stutters. During intense explosions, the frame rate drops below 30 fps for extended periods. Both consoles render the game internally at 1440p. While the standard PS5 relies on simple spatial upscaling, the PS5 Pro, thanks to PSSR, reconstructs a convincing 4K image and also features ray-traced shadows.
A 60 FPS mode would have destroyed the character of the game.
Technically, a 60 FPS mode wouldn't have been entirely impossible, according to Digital Foundry. However, Rockstar would have had to drastically reduce the graphics quality and the vibrancy of the simulation. The review doesn't reveal whether such compromises were ever tested internally.

SOURCE wikigtavi.com (GTA 6 RAGE Engine Explained: History, Tech and What Is New):
Every Rockstar game since a 2006 table tennis title has run on RAGE, the engine Rockstar San Diego built after EA bought RenderWare. This guide traces it from GTA IV through GTA V and RDR2 to the ray-traced lighting Digital Foundry found in GTA 6.
- RAGE was born when EA bought Criterion in 2004; Rockstar built its own engine at the former Angel Studios and shipped it first in Table Tennis on May 23, 2006.
- GTA V used a deferred renderer with a five-target G-buffer; RDR2 moved to physically based materials; GTA V Enhanced trialled ray tracing in 2025.
- Physics comes from Bullet and character balance from NaturalMotion’s Euphoria, first shipped in GTA IV; GTA 6 shows the same reactive behaviour.
- In GTA 6, Digital Foundry finds ray tracing central to lighting and reflections while sun shadows stay on refined shadow maps.
What RAGE Is and Why Rockstar Built It
RAGE stands for Rockstar Advanced Game Engine, the in-house technology every major Rockstar game has run on since 2006. It is built and maintained by the RAGE Technology Group inside Rockstar San Diego, the studio that used to be Angel Studios, and it grew out of that studio’s own Angel Game Engine. Unlike Unreal or Unity it is not licensed to anyone else, which is why you will never see a RAGE logo on a non-Rockstar game and why the company rarely talks about it by name.
The reason it exists is a corporate accident. Through the PlayStation 2 era Rockstar built GTA III, Vice City and San Andreas on RenderWare, a licensed engine made by Criterion Games. Obbe Vermeij, technical director at Rockstar North in those years, has said the hardest technical challenge on GTA III was streaming, loading the city off the disc as the player moved, and that Adam Fowler wrote the code. When it could not be made any faster, the artists re-laid Portland’s long main road to slow players down, and drag on vehicles was raised by about 5% in other trouble spots. In 2004 Electronic Arts bought Criterion, which put the technology under Rockstar’s biggest open-world rival, and Take-Two already owned a studio with its own engine: Angel Studios, bought in 2002 and renamed Rockstar San Diego. Rockstar spun up the RAGE Technology Group there, started from the Angel engine, and set about building something that could stream a city on the hardware that was coming next. Co-founder Jamie King remembers stepping off a plane from Rockstar Vienna to hear Sam Houser tell him that EA had just bought RenderWare and Rockstar needed an engine of its own. Our development history covers the studio side of that decade; this guide is about the technology.
A Ping-Pong Game as the Test Bed
The first RAGE game was not a GTA. It was Rockstar Games Presents Table Tennis, released for Xbox 360 on May 23, 2006 and ported to Wii the following year. At the time it looked like a strange detour for the studio behind San Andreas; in hindsight it was the smartest possible way to learn a new console generation and a new engine without a thousand-person production riding on it. A table tennis match is two realistic human characters, one room, fast animation and nothing else, which is exactly the list of things a new engine needs to prove first. Critic Oli Welsh, looking back on the game’s twentieth anniversary, described it as a focused test bed for rendering realistic human characters.
